focus_relevance_note: Earliest template for guitar-vs-voice dual protagonist: Ritchie Blackmore's escalating solo and Ian Gillan's banshee falsetto cycle through 10+ minutes in counterpoint, each amplifying the other's intensity. The song cycles through the dialectic multiple times — neither protagonist 'wins.'

First canonical two-movement song: the volcanic Clapton/Allman dual-guitar vocal section followed by an entirely separate piano coda (Jim Gordon). Two structural protagonists inhabiting the same piece without sharing a foreground — the earliest documented split into aria-then-coda form in rock.

Multi-section epic where Page's guitar solo (5:34–6:44) yields to Plant's unaccompanied vocal epilogue — Page chose to omit his planned guitar ending because Plant's voice alone had more impact. A documented decision about which protagonist should have the final word.

Bridge node: the synth drone functions as the absent 'other voice' against which Daltrey's final scream is the vocal answer. Protagonist duality exists but is machine-vs-human rather than guitar-vs-voice — present in the lineage as a structural sibling, not a direct ancestor.

Textbook dual-movement song: Ronnie Van Zant's slow ballad vocal followed by an extended guitar dual-solo coda (Allen Collins + Gary Rossington). The coda was added to give Van Zant vocal rest — guitar takes over the protagonist role by necessity, then claims it permanently.

Canonized the suite-structure and made the guitar solo explicitly vocal: Brian May described wanting to 'sing a verse on the guitar,' positioning the solo as an aria protagonist in its own right. The 9-bar guitar solo bridges ballad to operatic section — guitar as transitional voice between two human-voice movements.

Three named protagonists: Roger Waters (verses), David Gilmour (choruses + two guitar solos), and Gilmour's guitar as a third. Waters and Gilmour are literally different characters in the Wall narrative. Gilmour's two solos are structurally positioned as responses after the choral climaxes — the guitar enters when the voice has no more words.

Metal's foundational dual-protagonist song: Hetfield's confessional vocal sections alternate with Hammett's escalating solos across 6:55. Hammett's first solo mirrors Hetfield's harmonic territory before diverging — the guitar initially speaks in the same register as the voice, then claims its own language.

Bridge node: extends the Fade to Black template to its logical extreme — the final third of the song drops all vocal completely, leaving guitar and drums as the sole protagonists for the climax. Hetfield becomes a rhythm guitarist to support Hammett's lead. Present as structural escalation before the anchor, not a separate pillar.

Anchor — the 7:30–9:00 section is where Axl Rose's final vocal plea and Slash's guitar solo simultaneously occupy the foreground, not in sequence but in counterpoint: both protagonists present at once, the aria and the solo finally sharing the same moment. Rose's liner notes thank Slash by name for 'the killer guitar melodies' that realised his vision.

The public-facing statement of the Axl/Slash dialectic: multiple Slash solos across nine minutes, the third (improvised) as the song's emotional apex. Rose's orchestral string arrangement frames the vocal as an aria. The longest song to enter the top ten of the Billboard Hot 100 at the time — the dual-protagonist form proven commercially viable at maximum scale.

Structural inversion of the dual-protagonist formula: Hetfield solos himself, Hammett is absent. The dialectic collapses into monologue — one person plays both the aria and the guitar protagonist. This inversion reveals the structural assumption of every other node: that voice and solo are different characters, played by different people.

Chinese rock's translation of the Western dual-protagonist structure: Dou Wei's vocal and the lead guitar work enact the same aria↔solo dialectic, but mediated through Chinese musical sensibility and language. The 1.5-million-copy debut album documented that the form travelled across cultural contexts intact.

Britpop heir to the arena-rock dual-protagonist structure: Liam Gallagher's detached vocal delivers the verses; the 7:27 track opens into a sustained Noel Gallagher/Paul Weller guitar outro that stretched to 5+ additional minutes live. The Liam/Noel sibling tension mirrors the Axl/Slash composer-vocalist-versus-guitarist dynamic.

Conscious suite-form descendant of Bohemian Rhapsody: Radiohead stitched three separate fragments together in the manner of Mercury's three-songs approach. Yorke (vocal) and Jonny Greenwood (lead guitar) are dual protagonists across three shifting movements. Documented Queen lineage makes the descent explicit.

song: 丸ノ内サディスティック
focus_relevance_note: J-pop translation of the aria↔solo dialectic into compact form: Shiina Ringo's vocal (breath-as-texture, syllabically dense) and the guitar solo are dual voices within a pop frame rather than an epic one. The guitar solo explicitly mirrors the keyboard harmonica phrase from the intro — solo as restatement of a previously-heard voice.

Most explicit Bohemian Rhapsody descendant in 2000s rock: Ray Toro documented that the band consciously set out to write a song like Bohemian Rhapsody; Brian May performed with MCR at a documented 2007 concert. Gerard Way's multi-register vocal and Toro's guitar are the dual protagonists across a multi-section structure.

Inversion of the standard aria↔solo sequence: the song opens with 2:03 of pure guitar instrumental before Bellamy's vocal enters. Guitar-first, voice-second — a structural mirror of the form that reveals it by reversing it. The second half of the song was originally a separate piece appended by the band, echoing the assembly method of both Layla and Bohemian Rhapsody.
